meta.title: Post-quantum Nostr identities
meta.description: Check whether a Nostr profile can receive post-quantum encrypted messages, and see how post-quantum keys are derived from an existing seed phrase.

hero.title: Post-quantum Nostr
hero.subtitle: Every encrypted message on Nostr today can be decrypted later by anyone who recorded it. Post-quantum keys derived from the seed phrase you already have close that gap - without changing your identity.

checker.title: Check a profile
checker.subtitle: Enter an npub to see whether it publishes post-quantum keys, and whether those keys can be trusted.
checker.placeholder: npub1... or a hex public key
checker.earlyNotice: This proposal is new, so almost no profile publishes these keys yet. An empty result means the identity has not adopted it - not that the check failed.

result.invalidInput: That is not a valid npub or public key
result.notFoundDetail: This identity has no attestation event on the relays we queried. Messages to it can only be encrypted with classic cryptography, which a quantum computer would be able to decrypt retroactively.

how.title: How it works
how.subtitle: Three ideas, none of which require a relay to change.

seed.title: Keys derived as siblings, not children
seed.body: Your post-quantum keys come from the same BIP-39 seed as your Nostr key, expanded separately. Neither key is derived from the other. That matters: if a post-quantum key were derived from your private key, an attacker who broke your Nostr key would simply repeat the derivation and get it too. Because the seed derivation is one-way, breaking your Nostr key reveals nothing about it.

attestation.title: Published in their own event
attestation.body: The public keys live in a dedicated replaceable event rather than in your profile metadata. Clients rebuild profile metadata from the fields they recognise, so an unknown key would silently disappear the first time you edited your display name somewhere else - and you would never know.

wrap.title: Carried inside today's gift wrap
wrap.body: The post-quantum payload travels inside the existing NIP-44 and NIP-59 layers, combined with the classic key rather than replacing it. Relays need no changes, and clients that have not implemented any of this are unaffected.

limits.title: What this does not do
limits.body: This protects the confidentiality of messages sent from now on, permanently, even against someone who records them today and breaks the cryptography later. It does not stop a quantum attacker from forging events in your name, because events are still signed with secp256k1. Fixing that means migrating signatures, which is a separate and much larger change.

problems.keyLength: The {alg} key is {bytes} bytes; {expected} were expected. This attestation is malformed.
problems.noAlgTags: The attestation carries no keys at all.
problems.noKem: No {alg} encapsulation key, so this identity cannot receive post-quantum encrypted messages.
problems.derivedWeakSeed: Claims seed-derived keys from a {bits}-bit seed. The specification requires 256 bits for derived keys; a weaker seed must be published as an independent key instead.
problems.derivedMissingSeedStrength: Claims seed-derived keys but does not state the seed strength, so the claim cannot be checked.
problems.missingPop: The {alg} key is published without a proof of possession, so there is no evidence the holder controls it.
problems.popFailed: The proof of possession does not verify. Do not trust these keys.

faq.title: Questions about the checker
faq.subtitle: What it looks up, and what to do with the answer.

what.a: It looks up the identity’s kind:10203 attestation on public relays and validates it: are the key lengths right for ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87, does the origin match the declared seed strength, and does the proof of possession verify.

notfound.q: Why does it say no attestation was found?
notfound.a: Because that identity has not published one. There is no fallback and no guessing: without a published ML-KEM key there is no way to send them a post-quantum message, and reporting anything softer would invite a silent downgrade to classic encryption.

proof.a: A secp256k1 signature proves someone published those bytes, not that they hold the matching post-quantum secrets. So the ML-DSA key counter-signs a message binding the npub and both public keys together. ML-KEM cannot sign, which is why this is also what gives the encryption key a possession proof.

getone.q: How do I get post-quantum keys?
getone.a: Derive them from the 24-word seed phrase you already have — no new backup, and the same words still restore everything. The Nostr WoT extension can publish the attestation for you, or the guide walks through doing it offline from the command line.

standard.a: It is a proposal, developed jointly by Nostr WoT and QuantaKrypto, built on the finalised NIST standards FIPS 203 and FIPS 204. It is implemented and running rather than theoretical, which is the point of the live chat demo.

tools.title: Two tools
tools.subtitle: One checks somebody else. The other lets you watch the whole thing happen.

check.title: Check a profile
check.body: Look up any npub and see whether it has published post-quantum keys, whether the key lengths are right, and whether possession is proven.

chat.title: Live post-quantum chat
chat.body: Two identities register on public relays and exchange real ML-KEM encrypted messages. Take any event apart layer by layer and see exactly what a relay stores.
